title: Kabir: the true warrior
hookLine: the brave one is the one who fights for the helpless and does not leave the field (Maru, Kabir, ang 1105)

cards: A school hallway. A bigger kid has cornered a smaller one, and a small crowd watches, phones out, nobody moving. Then one kid, not the biggest, not the toughest, steps between them and says: that's enough.
Everyone in that hallway knows, instantly, who the brave one was. Not the loudest. The one who stood up for someone who couldn't.
Kabir, the weaver who sang of one light, has a couplet about exactly that kind of courage. Sikhs have loved it for centuries.

teach.h: THE DRUM SOUNDS, THE LINE IS DRAWN.
teach.b: On Ang 1105, among Kabir's saloks in Rag Maru, come two short couplets. The first sets the scene: the war drum sounds in the sky, the battle line is drawn, now is the time to fight.

teach.h: SOORAA — THE ONE WHO STANDS FOR DEEN.
teach.b: The second gives the definition: sooraa so pahichaaneeai ju larai deen ke het; purjaa purjaa kat marai kabahoo na chhaadai khet.
Know that one as a hero who fights for the sake of the deen; who may be cut to pieces, but never leaves the field. Slow down on deen. In Punjabi it can mean the poor, the humble, the helpless.
It's also close to an Arabic word, din, meaning faith.

teach.h: DEEN: THE HELPLESS, AND WHAT'S RIGHT.
teach.b: Commentators read it both ways, and both have been loved: the hero fights for the helpless, and for what is right.

What the verse doesn't praise is just as clear: not the one who fights for loot or fame or land, not the one who wins. The one who stands for those who can't, and doesn't run. Why would a peaceful weaver sing this?
Many Sikhs read the field two ways. The outer field: standing up for the weak, as later Sikhs, soldier-saints, would do.

teach.h: THE OUTER FIELD AND THE INNER.
teach.b: And the inner field, where the enemies are the five thieves, lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride, and staying on the field means not giving up on yourself.
Either way, courage here isn't about strength. It's about who you're standing for, and whether you stay.

how: Kabir's couplet on the true hero is often recited and sung by Sikhs, and it's commonly linked with the Sikh ideal of the saint-soldier who protects the defenseless.

o: a Sikh general who led soldier-saints to war
a Sufi teacher who taught never to fight
a Bhagat whose hero fights for the helpless

games.q: inside Kabir's couplet — tap the pairs.

s: Kabir's hero is the one who wins the most battles
the hero is the one who fights for the helpless and doesn't leave the field.
the word deen can be read as the helpless or as faith
many Sikhs also read the field as an inner battle
against the five thieves: lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride.

games.q: the drum sounds and the line is drawn. in Kabir's couplet, how do you know who the real hero is?
o: the one who wins the most loot.
the one who fights for the helpless and never leaves the field.
the one with the loudest war cry.
games.why: sooraa so pahichaaneeai ju larai deen ke het: courage is about who you stand for, and whether you stay.

practice: Think of one small thing that needs someone to stand up for it: a coworker talked over in meetings, a friend mocked in a group chat, a neighbor who can't carry their groceries, a quiet wrong you've been walking past.
Picture yourself stepping in, calmly, not with anger, just with steadiness. Then rest with the breath, steady on the field.

wordCard.voice: Kabir. Here, his couplet in Maru: the true hero fights for the helpless, and for what's right, and never leaves the field.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: soora, the hero, the brave one; Kabir defines him by whom he fights for.

carryVoice: Your line: fight for the helpless. The field can be outer or inner. Day two hundred fifty-five is yours.
